passages.text: While Peter was discussing these things, one of the advance party came in from Antioch ..........., saying to Peter, “My master, I want you to know that Simon, publicly performing many wonders in Antioch and calling you a magician and a sorcerer, prepared them for such hatred that everyone longed, upon your coming into the city there, to take a taste of your very flesh. Therefore we, the advance party, together with our brothers whom you had placed with Simon, seeing the city roaring loudly against you, secretly gathered in the same place and considered what we should do. While we were at a loss, Cornelius the centurion arrived, sent by Caesar to the governor of the province—the one whom the Lord healed in Caesarea when he was possessed by a demon. We secretly sent for Cornelius, and he learned from us the reason for our despondency. When asked to help, he most eagerly promised to frighten Simon and drive him away, provided we assisted him in his undertaking. When we readily promised to do everything, he said, ‘While I, through many friends, secretly spread word around that I have come to arrest him, and claim that I am searching for him—since Caesar, having killed many magicians and learned what concerns him, sent me to search for him, so that he may punish him as he did the magicians before him—let your people who are with him also report back, as though they have heard secretly from somewhere that I was sent to arrest him. Perhaps, hearing this, he will be frightened and flee.’ Since, then, we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way. For, having heard many of the outsiders telling him privately, doing him great favors, and also our insiders who had been planted there, and as though he had received advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw. So he fled Antioch with Athenodorus and has come here, as we have heard. Therefore we advise you not yet to set foot in that city, until we see whether, in his absence, they will be able to forget the slander against you.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun identifies those who go ahead. “One of those who had gone ahead” is a less collective alternative. A military role or formal title is not added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling you a magician and a sorcerer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both accusations are retained. γόης can mean a conjurer, sorcerer, or deceiving charlatan; the magical context supports “sorcerer,” without independently confirming either accusation as true.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς γλίχεσθαι πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου.
lexical_decisions.chosen: everyone longed, upon your coming into the city there, to take a taste of your very flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The current selected prefix has singular genitive ἐπιδημήσαντος, understood circumstantially with the addressee Peter as the visitor identified by the later σου. The nominal “your coming” preserves the aorist participle’s completed-arrival perspective without asserting that the future arrival has already happened. The feminine τὴν has an implicit location, naturally the city discussed here and explicitly named later; the English supplies “city,” but no Greek noun is restored or inserted. The now articular τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν permits postposed αὐτῶν to agree with σαρκῶν intensively, “the flesh itself,” not as the possessive “their flesh.” The unchanged σου supplies Peter as possessor; English “your very flesh” represents that reading. The English repeats “your” to identify both the visitor and flesh-owner as the same addressed man; it does not claim that two Greek pronouns are printed or that both syntactic links are uniquely settled. A possessive reading of αὐτῶν, “their flesh,” remains formally possible but leaves its relation to σου difficult in this context. This is a candidate analysis of the curated whole construction, not acceptance inferred merely from the existence of a critical proposal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπὸ σοῦ τῷ Σίμωνι ὑποβεβλημένων ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: our brothers whom you had placed with Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement is done by Peter, expressed through ὑπὸ σοῦ, and involves the community’s brothers with Simon. ὑποβάλλω here can imply covertly planting or introducing them, as the later insiders description suggests. No additional act of conversion or betrayal is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one whom the Lord healed in Caesarea when he was possessed by a demon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine relative can refer to the immediately preceding provincial governor, or reach back to Cornelius. The English “the one” leaves that personal referent unassigned rather than uniquely choosing either man. δαιμονῶντα is rendered in the author’s demonic category, not converted into a modern diagnosis.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περικομποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: While I, through many friends, secretly spread word around that I have come to arrest him, and claim that I am searching for him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected περικομποῦντος is Wieseler’s explicitly printed editorial proposal, meaning proclaiming or spreading a claim around; it is not the former περισκοποῦντος, looking around or examining. The perfect infinitive ἐληλυθέναι now supplies the content of that announcement, “that I have come,” with εἰς σύλληψιν expressing its stated purpose. The accompanying φάσκοντος gives the claim that Cornelius is searching for Simon. The main text connects the genitive-absolute circumstance with the later imperative asking their people to report back; the printed intervening stop is separately disclosed. The words are Cornelius’s proposed announcement in the reported plan, not independent confirmation of an actual arrest order.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἕτερόν τι ποιεῖν ἐπενοήσαμεν, ὅμως οὕτως ἐγένετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: Since, then, we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the opening ἐπεί and the contrasting ὅμως are preserved, without changing the printed conjunction to a different Greek word. A more idiomatic contextual interpretation is “Although we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way”; that shifts ἐπεί toward a concessive English link rather than its causal “since,” and is not uniquely established.

The source’s great-favor language is retained as describing the outside informants’ service to Simon. Unlike a different reading with ὡς, the selected εἰς phrase is not automatically translated “as though” doing favors.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: whether, in his absence, they will be able to forget the slander against you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural subject of δυνήσονται is the people of the city under discussion; the slander is the genitive object of forgetting, not a nominative subject that itself subsides. The unchanged sigma-form ὑπολῆσαι is interpreted through Sophocles’s directly cited lexical evidence under ὑπολανθάνω, “forget,” rather than the cessation lemma ὑπολήγω. This is a fresh rendering of the supplied Greek using a dictionary gloss, not an adaptation of an older English passage translation.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints an eleven-dot gap between Antioch and the participle “saying.” Exactly eleven dots remain in the main English. No missing participle, arrival formula, or other lost word is restored from another edition.

source_issues.source_quote: πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν
source_issues.issue: This passage uses the human-authorized, independently image-checked Greek prefix proposed by F. Wieseler, Adnotationes criticae, 1859, printed page 326 / PDF page 347. The former selected Lagarde prefix is preserved exactly here: πάντα ἄνθρωπον τῶν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημησάντων σαρκῶν. The selected prefix is: πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν. Wieseler’s printed proposal is followed by cett.; ONLY the explicitly verified Greek prefix was adopted, not an invented expansion of that abbreviation. The remaining αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου is unchanged from Lagarde. Wieseler also proposes τῇ ἐκεῖ as an alternative to the destination construction; it is noted as another editorial proposal, not silently selected. These are scholarly conjectures, not new manuscript collations or recovery of a uniquely established original. The prior candidate could not securely link the uncurated plural-participle/flesh sequence; the present interpretation is reassessed on the documented changed prefix and the articular flesh phrase, with the remaining attachments disclosed rather than invented. Fresh independent review must judge the entire construction.

source_issues.source_quote: φυγαδεύειν αὐτόν. ἐάν γε αὐτοῦ τῷ ἐγχειρήματι ὑπουργήσωμεν.
source_issues.issue: The English attaches the condition “provided we assisted him” to Cornelius’s promise despite the selected edition’s full stop before ἐάν. The Greek punctuation is not changed or labelled an OCR error; no missing words are restored.

source_issues.source_quote: κολάσῃ. καὶ οἱ ὑμέτεροι οἱ συνόντες αὐτῷ
source_issues.issue: The English continues the initial genitive-absolute circumstance of spreading an announcement into the later imperative asking their people to report back, despite the printed stop after κολάσῃ. This makes the relation explicit without supplying a new main verb to the initial clause or deleting the source period. An alternative presentation can leave the earlier circumstance as a marked sentence fragment before the command; the continuous English is preferred because the later imperative supplies the action coordinated with Cornelius’s proposed announcement.

The verified Lagarde print has the eight-letter sigma-form ὑπολῆσαι, with circumflex, and it is retained unchanged. Independently checked primary lexical evidence is E.A. Sophocles, Greek Lexicon of the Roman and Byzantine Periods, 1900, printed page 1121 / PDF page 1147: under ὑπο-λανθάνω = λανθάνω it explicitly cites “Clementin. 461 A ὑπολῆσαι, to forget.” The accent in the lexicon’s quoted form remains uncertain in the independent image reading, possibly circumflex or acute (ὑπολήσαι); that uncertainty does not alter the independently verified Lagarde accent or the sigma. The lexicon attests an interpretation of this unusual form but does not establish ordinary classical morphology. The expected cessation-form comparison ὑπολῆξαι would be hypothetical and is NOT adopted; no Greek emendation or identification with ὑπολήγω is made. The supplied evidence request, response, and receipt hashes bind the supporting dictionary check in the generation packet. Fresh independent translation review is still required.

The selected word is Wieseler’s independently image-verified critical proposal, printed page 327 / PDF page 348: περικομποῦντος. The former selected Lagarde word is retained exactly here as provenance: περισκοποῦντος. The change is editorial and conjectural, not a newly verified manuscript reading. It replaces the looking-around/examining sense with announcing-around, permitting the perfect infinitive to express the announced arrival. No other wording or printed punctuation is silently altered, and independent source-and-translation review remains required.
